stem: Your API reads user profile data on every request. DB latency is 180ms. You want sub-10ms. Which strategy is most appropriate?
explanation: Redis with the cache-aside pattern is the right tool: on a cache miss, fetch from DB and write to Redis with a TTL; subsequent reads hit Redis in ~1ms. A read replica reduces DB load but doesn't eliminate the 180ms latency. NoSQL and connection pools address different bottlenecks.
options: Introduce Redis with a cache-aside pattern
Increase the database connection pool size
author: codearena-core

stem: Which cache eviction policy is best when your access pattern follows the Pareto principle — 20% of keys are accessed 80% of the time?
explanation: LRU (Least Recently Used) is ideal for Pareto / temporal locality patterns. Frequently accessed keys stay hot in cache; infrequently accessed keys expire naturally. LFU is also good but requires more metadata. FIFO and Random ignore access frequency entirely.
author: codearena-core

stem: You're designing a system where data is written once and read millions of times (e.g. a product catalogue). What database optimisation should you prioritise?
explanation: Read-heavy, write-rare workloads benefit most from aggressive indexing and read replicas. Indexes trade write overhead (negligible here since writes are rare) for drastically faster reads. A CDN layer is also valid for static data but is a caching strategy, not a DB optimisation.
author: codearena-core

stem: A payment service needs to process transactions. What property must your message queue guarantee to avoid double-charging customers?
explanation: Exactly-once delivery guarantees each message is processed precisely once — critical for financial transactions. At-least-once (common default) may cause duplicate processing. At-most-once may drop messages. Ordering matters for some workflows but doesn't prevent duplicates.
author: codearena-core

stem: According to the CAP theorem, during a network partition a distributed system must choose between which two properties?
explanation: CAP theorem: a distributed system can guarantee at most two of Consistency, Availability, and Partition tolerance. Since network partitions are unavoidable in practice, the real choice during a partition is between Consistency (return an error rather than stale data) and Availability (return best-effort data, possibly stale).
author: codearena-core

stem: What is the key difference between horizontal scaling and vertical scaling?
explanation: Vertical scaling (scale-up) means upgrading a single machine — more CPU, RAM, or faster disks. Horizontal scaling (scale-out) means adding more machines and distributing load. Horizontal scaling has no theoretical ceiling and is more resilient to single-node failures, but requires your application to support distribution (stateless design, load balancers, etc.).
options: Horizontal = faster CPUs; Vertical = more servers
Horizontal = adding more servers; Vertical = upgrading existing servers
They are the same — different names for the same concept
Horizontal = database scaling only; Vertical = application scaling only
author: codearena-core
